온프레미스 Product · Employee · Experience · AI Analytics 플랫폼

🇰🇷 홍보 페이지 · 🇺🇸 English Page · 🌐 전체 서비스 · 💖 Sponsor

--- ## 현재 제공 범위 - JavaScript SDK: Event 발생 시점 Context snapshot, DEV/STG/PRD, Event Contract version, Release context, Page View/SPA/custom event, identify, session/visitor, first-touch UTM, click/form/error, Core Web Vitals·Resource Error RUM, fail-closed consent, cookieless, batch, Beacon, offline queue - Durable Collector: `POST /collect/v1/events`, 환경별 계약 `allow/warn/reject`, domain/key 검증, 중복 제거, 수집 전 값 기반 PII Detect/Mask/Reject, Cardinality Guard, PostgreSQL inbox 기반 비동기 적재 및 작업별 savepoint 재시도 - 방문자 추적: SSO로 연결된 모든 기기를 한 사람으로 합친 세션 단위 타임라인, User·부서·페이지·이벤트 검색, 식별 시점, 커서 페이징, 교차 서비스 활동, 추적 기록 Markdown - 이상 감지: 같은 요일 최근 8주 중위수·MAD 기반 robust z-score 감시와 신규·지속·회복 알림 상태 관리로 같은 이상을 반복 통보하지 않는 알림 - 기여도: 단일 터치(first/last/last-non-direct)와 다중 터치(선형·시간 감쇠·위치 기반) 채널 배분, SSO 기반 교차 서비스 배분, 관여 전환, 평균 경로 길이, Metric Goal 착지 예측 - 방문자 인사이트: 전기간 자동 비교 KPI, 신규·재방문 구조, 채널 그룹 분류, 진입 페이지 이탈, 방문 빈도·최근성, 기기 격차, 우선순위 인사이트와 실행 대상 Segment, Markdown 즉시 복사·다운로드·정기 배달 - 분석: 첫 화면 「지금 봐야 할 것」(이상 감지·Goal 미달 전망 통합), Overview, Realtime, Acquisition, Pages, Events, Visitors, Sessions, Cohort/Retention, Site·Cross-Site Business Journey, Workspace Roll-Up, Feature/Search/Frustration, Experiment, Web Vitals/Error/Release Impact, Insight/Root Cause, Ecommerce, User Timeline - 거버넌스: 버전형 Event Contract와 CI 검증, Formula 지원 Semantic Metric Registry, Metric Goal, Event Catalog·Lineage, DEV/STG/PRD 정책, Tracking Health Score, PII·Cardinality 이슈, Adoption 대상자 분모 - 비밀값 관리: `MOMENTO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` 기반 AES-256-GCM 저장, 재기동 후 키 재조회, 키 교체용 이전 키 병행과 재암호화, 설치 진단(CSP·허용 도메인·환경·적재 파이프라인) - 관리: 운영 준비도·품질 지표·우선순위 조치함을 갖춘 역할 기반 관리 센터, `Ctrl/Cmd+K` 명령 팔레트, Site/Tracking Key, Keycloak OIDC(PKCE), RBAC, 사용자, 개인정보, 사이트별 Retention, CIDR 망 이름, Event Schema/Conversion, Custom Dimension, Audit - 고급 분석: Segment 비교 Funnel·Retention·Web Vitals/오류 경험 비교(전체 대비 완주율 격차와 이탈 단계 지목), Exact/Fast/Preview Query Cost Guard, 중첩 AND/OR Segment Registry, Segment 기반 Query/Funnel, 사용자·세션 전환율, 참여 기준과 활동량이 포함된 Session 요약, 저장된 Exploration - 개인화: Profile, password, 개인 API key 발급·회전·폐기 - AI/연동: Model·Agent·MCP·Tool 사용량/성공률/지연/토큰/비용, 완전 오프라인 자연어 분석, 22개 Analytics MCP 도구, REST/OpenAPI, Raw CSV/NDJSON export - Action: 보안 Host Allowlist 기반 Scheduled Report와 Segment 집계를 Webhook, Confluence, Mail Gateway, 사내 메시지, AI Agent로 전달 - name: Offline image release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  # A tag push can go unscheduled during a platform incident, and a release that
  # was missed then could not be produced afterwards: the only trigger was the
  # push itself, which does not repeat. This accepts the tag to build.
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: Tag to build and release, for example v0.31.6
        required: true
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      # The tag being released, from the dispatch input when there is one and from
      # the pushed ref otherwise, so the steps below need no branching.
      #
      # Deliberately not named GITHUB_REF_NAME: the runner sets its own value for
      # the reserved variables regardless of what a job declares, so shadowing it
      # produced a run whose env block displayed the tag while the shell saw
      # "main" and tried to release a tag by that name.
      RELEASE_TAG: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          # A dispatched run starts from the default branch, so the tag has to be
          # checked out explicitly or the image would be built from main.
          ref: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref }}
      # The commit comes from the tree that was checked out, not from GITHUB_SHA.
      # For a tag push they are the same. For a dispatch — which is how a missed
      # or half-published release is repaired — GITHUB_SHA is the branch the
      # workflow was dispatched against while the checkout above is the tag, so
      # the artifact was stamped with a commit it does not contain. Measured on
      # v0.33.7: the tag's own run reported 2a90aee80a9e and a dispatched rebuild
      # of the same tag reported b1216bf9052b, which is a commit that came after
      # it. The version endpoint exists so an operator can say what they are
      # running; a commit from another branch is worse than none.
      - name: Read the commit being released
        run: echo "RELEASE_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      # The image is named repository:tag and the archive is one word — the two
      # shapes an operator meets, kept deliberately parallel: momento:v0.34.2
      # loads out of momento-v0.34.2.tar.gz.
      - name: Build service image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --build-arg VERSION="${RELEASE_TAG#v}" \
            --build-arg COMMIT="${RELEASE_COMMIT}" \
            --build-arg BUILD_TIME="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
            -t "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}" .
      - name: Export offline image only
        run: |
          docker save "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}" | gzip -9 > "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz"
          sha256sum "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz" > "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256"
      # The artifact is the product for an offline deployment, and until now
      # nothing had ever loaded one and started it. This runs the archive that is
      # about to be published — not the image still in the local daemon — through
      # the install sequence the release notes give, so a tarball that cannot
      # start is never published.
      - name: Smoke test the offline artifact
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          # Loading from the archive is the point: it proves what a user receives.
          docker image rm "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
          gzip -dc "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz" | docker load
          sha256sum -c "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256"

          docker network create momento-smoke
          docker run -d --name smoke-pg --network momento-smoke \
            -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=smoke -e POSTGRES_DB=momento postgres:17-alpine
          for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
            docker exec smoke-pg pg_isready -U postgres >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
            sleep 2
          done

          docker run -d --name smoke-app --network momento-smoke -p 127.0.0.1:8099:8080 \
            -e MOMENTO_POSTGRES_DSN='postgres://postgres:smoke@smoke-pg:5432/momento?sslmode=disable' \
            -e MOMENTO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN='admin@example.com' \
            -e MOMENTO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD='smoke-test-password-long-enough' \
            -e MOMENTO_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)" \
            "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}"

          # Ready means the migrations ran and the database is reachable, which is
          # the part an operator cannot verify from the outside.
          ready=""
          for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
            if curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8099/health/ready | grep -q ready; then
              ready=yes
              break
            fi
            sleep 2
          done
          if [[ -z "$ready" ]]; then
            echo "::error title=Offline artifact does not start::/health/ready never answered"
            docker logs smoke-app || true
            exit 1
          fi

          # The archive has to be the version it is named after.
          reported=$(curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8099/api/v1/version)
          echo "version endpoint: $reported"
          if ! echo "$reported" | grep -q "\"version\":\"${RELEASE_TAG#v}\""; then
            echo "::error title=Wrong version in artifact::expected ${RELEASE_TAG#v}, got $reported"
            exit 1
          fi
          # And the commit it names has to be the tag's own, whichever trigger
          # built it. A rebuild of an old tag that reports today's branch head
          # sends anybody investigating to code the image does not contain.
          if ! echo "$reported" | grep -q "\"commit\":\"${RELEASE_COMMIT}\""; then
            echo "::error title=Wrong commit in artifact::expected ${RELEASE_COMMIT} for ${RELEASE_TAG}, got $reported"
            exit 1
          fi

          # The console is embedded in the binary, so a missing build would show
          # up here rather than in any API check.
          curl -fsS -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8099/
          # And the operator's first action has to work.
          curl -fsS -o /dev/null -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8099/api/v1/auth/login \
            -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
            -d '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"smoke-test-password-long-enough"}'
          echo "offline artifact started, reported ${RELEASE_TAG}, served the console and accepted the bootstrap login"
      - name: Collect smoke test logs on failure
        if: failure()
        run: docker logs smoke-app 2>&1 | tail -50 || true
      - name: Remove smoke test containers
        if: always()
        run: |
          docker rm -f smoke-app smoke-pg >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
          docker network rm momento-smoke >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      # Publishing has to be repeatable, because the reconciliation workflow exists
      # to repeat it. It dispatches this workflow for a tag whose release is
      # missing or has only one of its two assets — and `gh release create` fails
      # outright when a release already exists, so the half-published case it was
      # written to repair could never be repaired: every dispatch died on "a
      # release with the same tag name already exists" and left the release as it
      # found it. The same error turned a healthy release red whenever
      # reconciliation happened to look while the tag's own run was still
      # building.
      - name: Publish GitHub release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [[ -f ".github/release-notes/${RELEASE_TAG}.md" ]]; then
            NOTES=(--notes-file ".github/release-notes/${RELEASE_TAG}.md")
          else
            NOTES=(--generate-notes)
          fi
          if gh release view "$RELEASE_TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "::notice title=Release exists::$RELEASE_TAG is already published; uploading the artifacts in place."
            gh release upload "$RELEASE_TAG" \
              "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz" \
              "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256" \
              --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \
              --clobber
          else
            gh release create "$RELEASE_TAG" \
              "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz" \
              "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256" \
              --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \
              --title "Momento ${RELEASE_TAG}" \
              "${NOTES[@]}" \
              --verify-tag
          fi
          # Whichever path ran, the release has to end up with both artifacts.
          published=$(gh release view "$RELEASE_TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --json assets --jq '.assets | length')
          if [[ "$published" != "2" ]]; then
            echo "::error title=Release incomplete::$RELEASE_TAG has $published assets, expected the archive and its checksum"
            exit 1
          fi
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  # A push does not always get scheduled — a platform incident can drop the run
  # while leaving the release workflow to report a startup failure — and without a
  # manual trigger there is no way to verify a commit after the fact.
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # The analytical reports build SQL by hand, so the suite runs them against a real
    # PostgreSQL instance. A syntax or type error there is invisible to unit tests.
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ci
          POSTGRES_DB: momento
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres -d momento"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 3s
          --health-retries 20
    env:
      MOMENTO_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN: postgres://postgres:ci@127.0.0.1:5432/momento?sslmode=disable
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
          cache: true
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: |
            web/package-lock.json
            sdk/package-lock.json
      # The reports answer by running their independent reads at the same time, so
      # the handlers that build them share variables across goroutines. The race
      # detector is what says that sharing is correct; without it a report that
      # occasionally returned a half-filled answer would look like a flaky test.
      # It costs about ninety seconds here, because these tests wait on a database
      # rather than on the CPU.
      - run: go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/...
      - run: go vet ./cmd/... ./internal/...
      - run: go run golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest ./cmd/... ./internal/...
      - run: npm ci && npm audit && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build
        working-directory: sdk
      - run: npm ci && npm audit && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build
        working-directory: web
      - name: Build production image
        run: docker build --build-arg VERSION=ci --build-arg COMMIT=${GITHUB_SHA::12} -t momento:ci .
name: Release reconciliation

# A tag push is a one-shot trigger. Twice now a platform incident dropped it, and
# the result was a tag with no release that nobody would notice without looking:
# the tag is there, the version is announced, and the artifact an offline install
# needs does not exist. This reconciles the two on a schedule, so a missed release
# repairs itself instead of waiting to be discovered.
on:
  schedule:
    # Hourly, off the hour: the top of the hour is when scheduled jobs queue up
    # across GitHub and get delayed the most.
    - cron: "23 * * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  # Needed to dispatch the release workflow for a tag that is missing one.
  actions: write

jobs:
  reconcile:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          # Tags are the input to this job, so a shallow clone is not enough.
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Repair tags with no release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          now=$(date +%s)
          repaired=0
          # Newest first, and only recent tags: an old tag without a release was a
          # deliberate choice by then, and rebuilding it would be surprising.
          while read -r tag created; do
            [[ -z "$tag" ]] && continue
            age_days=$(( (now - created) / 86400 ))
            if (( age_days > 7 )); then
              break
            fi
            # A tag pushed in the last half hour is probably being released right
            # now: its own run builds an image and smoke tests the archive before
            # publishing, so for a few minutes the release genuinely does not
            # exist yet. Dispatching then produced a duplicate run that raced the
            # real one, and one of the two ended red on a release that was fine.
            # Nothing is lost by waiting — this runs every hour.
            age_minutes=$(( (now - created) / 60 ))
            if (( age_minutes < 30 )); then
              echo "$tag was pushed ${age_minutes}m ago; its own release run has not had time to finish."
              continue
            fi
            assets=$(gh release view "$tag" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --json assets --jq '.assets | length' 2>/dev/null || echo "missing")
            if [[ "$assets" == "2" ]]; then
              continue
            fi
            if [[ "$assets" == "missing" ]]; then
              echo "::warning title=Release missing::$tag has no release. Dispatching the release workflow."
            else
              # A release with the wrong number of assets is a half-finished run:
              # the archive and its checksum are published together or not at all.
              echo "::warning title=Release incomplete::$tag has a release with $assets assets, expected 2. Dispatching the release workflow."
            fi
            gh workflow run "Offline image release" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --ref "${{ github.ref_name }}" -f tag="$tag"
            repaired=$((repaired + 1))
          done < <(git for-each-ref --sort=-creatordate --format='%(refname:short) %(creatordate:unix)' 'refs/tags/v[0-9]*')

          if (( repaired == 0 )); then
            echo "Every tag from the last seven days has a complete release."
          else
            # Not a failure: the repair was dispatched and the next run verifies it.
            echo "::notice title=Releases dispatched::$repaired tag(s) were missing a complete release."
          fi

name: estimating-and-contingency
description: Produces a cost or effort estimate someone can defend — decomposing the work, choosing between analogous, parametric and bottom-up methods, documenting the basis and its assumptions, expressing confidence as a range, and sizing contingency and management reserve separately. Use this to build an estimate, challenge one you have been handed, work out why estimates keep coming in low, or decide how much reserve a portfolio actually needs.
---

# Estimating and contingency

An estimate is a claim about an uncertain future. Most organizations treat it as a commitment made
by whoever said the number, which is why estimates are padded, disbelieved, and padded again.

## Decompose before you estimate

Estimate the work, not the project. Break it down until each piece is small enough that someone who
would do it can picture doing it — usually a week or two of effort. Below that you are estimating
noise; above it you are guessing.

Two decomposition failures are worth naming. **Missing scope** is the larger one: integration,
data migration, environments, testing, documentation, training, and the coordination overhead of
everyone involved routinely go unestimated because nobody owns them. **Double-counted contingency**
is the other: padding inside every task, then adding a reserve on top of the padded total.

## Pick the method that matches what you know

- **Analogous** — scale from a comparable past effort. Fast, needs real history, and the comparison
  has to survive being stated out loud: what is genuinely similar and what is not.
- **Parametric** — a rate applied to a count. Cost per endpoint, per interface, per square foot,
  per test case. Credible only when the rate comes from your own data and the count is knowable.
- **Bottom-up** — estimate each decomposed piece and roll up. Most accurate, most expensive, and
  worth it once the work is understood well enough for the pieces to be real.

Use two methods and compare them where the number matters. When they disagree by more than a
quarter, one of them is built on an assumption nobody has stated.

## Write the basis down, because that is the durable part

The number is the least useful output. The basis of estimate is what lets someone re-estimate
later instead of starting over: what is included, what is explicitly excluded, the rates and
quantities used, the assumptions the number depends on, and who provided each input.

An estimate without a basis cannot be defended, cannot be updated, and cannot be learned from. When
the project comes in at double, the basis is what tells you whether the estimate was wrong or the
work changed — and those call for opposite responses.

## Express it as a range, and say what the range means

A single number is a forecast disguised as a fact. Give a range, and state the confidence: "we
would hit this eight times in ten" is a different commitment from "this is the best case."

Ranges narrow as work is understood, not as deadlines approach. Re-estimate at genuine information
points — after discovery, after the first integration, after the first delivered increment — and
publish the revision rather than quietly holding the old number.

## Separate contingency from management reserve

- **Contingency** covers the known unknowns inside the estimate: things that will vary, at a size
  you can bound. It belongs to the project and is drawn against as risks materialize.
- **Management reserve** covers scope nobody has thought of yet. It belongs to whoever governs the
  portfolio, not to the project team, and it is released deliberately.

Collapsing the two produces the familiar pattern where contingency is spent early on ordinary
variance and nothing remains for the thing that actually goes wrong.

## Why estimates keep coming in low

Optimism is real but it is rarely the main driver. The larger ones are structural: the estimate was
made before scope was understood and never revisited; the estimator knew the number that would be
accepted; only the happy path was estimated; or the organization punishes revised estimates more
than it punishes overruns, so nobody revises.

Fix the incentive before fixing the arithmetic. An organization that treats a re-estimate as a
failure will get accurate estimates from no one.

## Sources

`references/sources.md` in this skill lists the outside authorities that settle the questions
here — what each one is authoritative for, and what you may do with it. Check them before
answering on anything they cover, and cite what you used. Most are free to read and not free
to reproduce; the use note on each is binding.

## Never

- Present a point estimate for work nobody has decomposed.
- Add contingency to an estimate that already has padding inside every task.
- Let an estimate stand as a commitment without recording what it assumed.
- Cut an estimate to fit a budget and leave the scope unchanged. That is not an estimate, it is a
  decision to overrun, taken early and left unsaid.

name: implementation-planning
description: Turns a spec or requirement into a written plan a separate session or agent can execute, then drives that plan through review checkpoints. Use this before touching code on any multi-step task, when work needs handing to someone else, when a task keeps sprawling mid-implementation, or when a plan exists and needs executing in order with verification between steps.
---

# Implementation planning

## When a plan is worth writing

More than about three steps, more than one file of consequence, or any work that will be handed off.
Below that, planning costs more than it saves.

## Writing the plan

A plan is executable when someone who was not in the conversation can follow it without guessing.
That means every step names:

- **The change** — the file or surface, and what it should do afterward.
- **The proof** — the command that shows it worked. "Run the tests" is not a step; the exact
  invocation is.
- **The checkpoint** — whether a human reviews before the next step starts.

Order steps so the system is working at the end of each one. A plan whose midpoint is a broken build
cannot be paused, and every plan gets paused.

State up front what is **out of scope**. Plans fail by accretion far more often than by being wrong.

## Executing

- One step at a time, in order. Finish and verify before starting the next.
- **Stop at checkpoints.** The point of a checkpoint is that continuing without it is a mistake.
- When reality contradicts the plan, stop and amend the plan. Do not improvise past it silently —
  the plan is the shared state, and a stale plan is worse than none.
- Track status *in* the plan as you go, so an interrupted run can resume.

## Never

- Start writing code because the plan felt obvious. If it was obvious, writing it costs a minute.
- Mark a step done without running its proof.
- Expand scope mid-execution. Note it, finish the plan, then decide.

name: solution-exploration
description: Explores the problem and the range of possible approaches before any code is written — clarifying what is actually being asked, surfacing options with their tradeoffs, and converging on one. Use this at the start of any feature, component, or behavior change, when a request is ambiguous, when the first idea is the only idea on the table, or when a design decision needs pressure-testing before commitment.
---

# Solution exploration

The most expensive bugs are decisions, not defects. This runs before implementation, not instead of
it.

## Establish what is actually wanted

The stated request is a proposed solution wearing the clothes of a requirement. Get underneath it:

- What outcome does the person want? What breaks today without it?
- Who else touches this, and what do they assume about it now?
- What is explicitly **not** being asked for?
- How will we know it worked — the observable difference.

If the answers conflict, stop and resolve that first. Building the average of two requirements
satisfies neither.

## Generate genuinely different options

Two variations of the same idea are one option. Force real range:

- The smallest thing that could work.
- The version that assumes this doubles in scope next quarter.
- The version that requires no new moving parts.
- Buy, borrow, or do nothing.

For each: what it costs, what it forecloses, and what has to be true for it to be right.

## Converge

Recommend one and say why the others lost. A comparison that ends without a recommendation has
moved the work, not done it.

Name the assumption the recommendation rests on most heavily — that is where the plan will break if
it breaks.

## Never

- Present options you would not accept as padding around the one you want.
- Skip this because the task "is simple." Simple tasks take five minutes here.
- Let a preference stand in for a reason.

# Architecture

초기 배포는 PostgreSQL 하나로 운영되지만 수집과 분석 책임은 코드와 durable queue에서 분리됩니다.

```text
Browser SDK / HTTP API
  → stateless Go Collector (Environment + Contract + privacy validation)
  → PostgreSQL event_inbox (durable acceptance boundary)
  → Go Worker (privacy re-check, normalization, network classification)
  → PostgreSQL raw_events (single source of truth)
  → PostgreSQL sessions (deduplicated event-driven session summary)
  → Visitor Identity Graph + canonical User profile
  → Visitor/Session/Site-local Daily aggregates
  → Late Event / Administrator Aggregate rebuild queue
  → Semantic Metric + Goal + Query Cost Guard
  → Workspace/Product/Search/Experiment/RUM/AI Query APIs / MCP
  → React Console

Scheduled Report / Segment Aggregate
  → Host Allowlist + HTTP delivery adapter
  → Webhook / Confluence / Mail Gateway / Internal Message / AI Agent
```

Collector는 개인정보 필터가 적용된 Inbox commit 이후 `202 Accepted`를 반환합니다. 여러 Momento 컨테이너를 실행하면 `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`로 inbox 작업을 나누므로 Collector와 Worker를 함께 수평 확장할 수 있습니다. Worker는 작업마다 PostgreSQL savepoint를 두어 한 작업의 SQL 오류가 같은 batch의 정상 작업과 retry/dead-letter 기록을 중단하지 않게 합니다. 중복 `event_id`는 `(site_id, event_id)` unique key로 제거합니다.

`raw_events`는 불변 원본이고 `analytics_events` read model이 `(site, visitor_id) → user_id`의 결정적 연결을 적용합니다. 식별된 사용자는 `u:<user_id>`, 익명 사용자는 `v:<visitor_id>`로 namespace를 분리해 ID 충돌을 막습니다. 같은 SSO User ID를 가진 여러 브라우저와 로그인 전 Event는 하나의 사용자로 분석되며 fingerprint는 사용하지 않습니다. 최신 canonical User Property는 과거 익명 Event의 User-scope 부서·조직 차원에도 적용하지만 Raw Event 자체는 수정하지 않습니다.

`raw_events`에서 Segment, Funnel, Ecommerce, Visitor Timeline을 계산하며, 허용된 Dimension Registry만 SQL 표현식으로 변환합니다. Segment 정의는 중첩 JSON AST로 저장되어 SQL 원문을 입력받지 않습니다. `sessions`, `visitors`, `visitor_sessions`와 Site-local 일별 집계는 Raw Event insert가 실제로 성공한 경우에만 동일 transaction에서 upsert되므로 SDK 재시도에 의해 합계가 중복되지 않습니다. Overview의 Calendar-day Trend는 일별 집계를 사용하고 partial-day 요청은 Raw Event로 fallback합니다. Timestamp는 UTC로 저장하고 모든 Calendar Query는 Site의 IANA Timezone 경계로 변환합니다. 개인정보 삭제는 Inbox/Dead Letter, Raw Event, Identity/Visitor/Session/Daily 파생 데이터 재생성을 하나의 transaction으로 묶습니다.

v0.5부터 `environment`와 `contract_version`이 Raw Event의 거버넌스 경계입니다. 기존 Event는 PRD/Version 1로 승격되며 Daily Aggregate의 Key도 Environment를 포함합니다. Event Contract는 Draft/Active/Deprecated Version으로 보관되고 Collector는 환경 정책과 Contract 정책 중 더 엄격한 규칙을 적용합니다.

v0.6의 Semantic Metric은 제한된 JSON AST 안에서 Ratio, Metric Reference, Event/User/Session Property Filter와 최소 사용 횟수를 조합합니다. Metric Goal, Explorer, REST와 MCP가 같은 정의를 사용합니다. Query Guard는 실행 전에 기간·Dimension·Filter·Segment의 Complexity를 평가하고 Exact/Fast/Preview 정책을 적용하며 모든 실행을 `query_audit`에 기록합니다.

Collector는 durable Inbox 이전에 값 기반 PII Detector를 실행합니다. `mask`는 Email·전화·주민번호·Luhn 유효 카드번호·Credential을 치환하고, `reject`는 원문 Sample 없이 Detector 종류만 Data Quality Issue에 남깁니다. 한 시간 이상 늦게 도착한 Event는 Site-local 날짜의 재집계 Job을 중복 없이 생성하며 Maintenance Worker가 Raw Event에서 해당 범위를 다시 계산합니다.

Workspace Analytics는 SSO가 확인된 사용자를 `u:<user_id>`로 Site 간 결합하고 익명 사용자는 `s:<site_uuid>:v:<visitor_id>`로 Site 범위에 고정합니다. 따라서 Cross-Site Journey가 익명 ID 충돌로 잘못 연결되지 않습니다.

Data Quality 카운터는 Collector의 Received/Rejected와 Worker의 Accepted/Duplicate/Late/PII/Cardinality 상태를 분리해 기록합니다. Cardinality Registry에는 원문 Value 대신 SHA-256 digest만 저장합니다. 자동화 Worker는 관리자 설정이 활성화되고 Endpoint Host가 Allowlist에 정확히 일치할 때만 HTTP 요청을 수행하며 Redirect를 따르지 않습니다.

수십억 건 고도화 단계에서는 `settings.storage.engine`을 전환점으로 사용해 Worker의 sink를 ClickHouse로 추가합니다. Metadata와 audit, user, settings, durable inbox는 PostgreSQL에 유지하고 Raw Event 및 aggregate만 ClickHouse에 둡니다.

이 칸은 다섯 줄 자유 입력인데 「저장」 이 `!site || !form.name` 만 보았고
helperText 도 없었다. 그래서 깨진 JSON 으로 저장을 누르면 뮤테이션 안의
`JSON.parse(form.schemaText)` 가 던져 요청이 서버에 가지도 않는데, 사용자는
그 헛클릭 왕복을 한 번 치른 뒤에야 안내를 읽었다(브라우저로 재확인 — main
상태에서 클릭 뒤 서버에 도달한 POST 가 0건).

v0.34.57 이 그 뒤늦은 안내를 한국어로 만들었으니 남은 것은 그 문장을 누르기
전에 보여 주는 것뿐이다. cidrRule.ts·retentionRule.ts 선례대로 순수 모듈
schemaTextRule.ts 를 두고, adminErrors.ts 의 JSON 구문 안내와 칸 아래의
helperText 가 같은 상수(JSON_SCHEMA_RULE)를 쓰게 했다 — 글자는 그대로다.

판정은 구문만 본다. 서버는 Schema map[string]any 로 받아 배열·문자열·숫자를
400 으로 거절하지만 null 은 통과시키므로, '객체가 아니면 막는다' 는 규칙은
null 에서 화면을 서버보다 좁게 만든다. 「저장」 을 닫는 것이 이 칸에서
정당한 이유는 판정자가 서버가 아니라 화면 자신의 같은 JSON.parse 여서

/bin/bash -lc "cat > /mnt/c/Users/USER/projects/aidev/state/runs/2026-10-08-100236-Momento-improve/brief.md <<'EOF'
- 과제: [수정 과제·초안] 반복된 릴리즈 검증 실패의 현재 잔존 원인을 확인하고 해당 의존성·스크립트만 수정한다 (가치 5 / 위험 2 / 작업량 M)
- 왜: 자동 적재는 PR #29 CI 실패를 가리키지만 현재 main@0beff4c에는 #29 병합 및 fcf17ce의 golang.org/x/text v0.41.0 수정이 이미 있다. 실패 로그와 현재 실행 결과를 대조하여 이미 고친 문제를 되풀이하지 않고 남은 실패만 해결한다.
- 수용 기준: 1) 실패 실행 ID·단계·원인을 확인한다(현재 미확인). 2) 워크플로 게이트를 유지한 채 실제 잔존 원인만 수정한다. 3) 동일 검증 명령을 로컬에서 재현하고 수정 후 통과를 원장에 기록한다.
- 건드릴 파일: 미확정. 읽은 .github/workflows/ci.yml의 govulncheck 및 SDK·web 게이트, .github/workflows/release.yml의 Docker 빌드·아티팩트 smoke test, Dockerfile을 기준으로 최대 프로덕션 6파일 이내로 제한한다. go.mod에는 이미 x/text v0.41.0이 있다.
- 검증 명령: go run golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest ./cmd/... ./internal/... (CI 실제 명령, 정찰 실행 전). 실패 단계 확인 후 같은 명령을 확정한다.
- 위험과 피할 것: 워크플로 완화·감사 생략·재시도로 실패 숨기기 금지. 정찰은 코드 수정·커밋을 하지 않는다. 자동 실패 정보가 과거 상태일 가능성이 있으므로 이미 적용된 수정 중복 금지.
- 차선 후보: 기존 수정이 이미 유효하면 동일 실패의 재발 방지 검증·운영 문서 한 조각으로 한정한다. 신규 UI 개선으로 전환하지 않는다.
EOF"

## 2026-10-08
- 선택: 「JSON Schema」 칸이 저장 전에 JSON 구문 오류를 말한다 (순수 모듈 `schemaTextRule.ts`) (가치 3 / 위험 1 / 작업량 S)
- 결과: 성공
- 요약: 「JSON Schema」 는 다섯 줄 자유 입력인데 「저장」 이 `disabled={!site || !form.name}`(AdminPage.tsx:3815) 로 schemaText 를 아예 보지 않고 helperText 도 없었다. 그래서 깨진 JSON 으로 저장을 누르면 `mutationFn` 안의 `JSON.parse(form.schemaText)`(3745) 가 던져 **요청이 서버에 가지도 않는데**, 사용자는 그 헛클릭 왕복을 한 번 치른 뒤에야 안내를 읽었다 — 이 전제를 main 상태의 브라우저로 다시 증명했다(「저장」 `disabled: false`, 클릭 뒤 서버에 도달한 POST **0건**, 그러고 나서야 Alert 이 그 한국어 문장을 보인다). v0.34.57 이 그 뒤늦은 안내를 한국어로 만들었으니 남은 것은 그 문장을 **누르기 전에** 보여 주는 것뿐이다. `cidrRule.ts`·`retentionRule.ts` 선례대로 순수 모듈 `web/src/pages/schemaTextRule.ts` 를 새로 두고(`CIDRJudgement` 와 같은 모양의 `SchemaTextJudgement`, 본체는 `JSON.parse` 를 try/catch 로 한 번 돌리는 것뿐), `adminErrors.ts:352` 의 하드코딩 문장을 그 모듈의 `JSON_SCHEMA_RULE` **import** 로 바꿨다(글자는 그대로 — 기존 adminErrors 테스트가 그 문장을 글자 그대로 보고, 특히 `test("코드가 붙은 실패는 JSON 구문 안내로 가로채이지 않는다")` 와 `switch` 앞의 `!code` 가드 분기는 손대지 않았다). `AdminPage.tsx` 는 `judgeSchemaText(form.schemaText)` 를 한 번 계산해 TextField 에 `error`/`helperText` 를 주고 「저장」 에 `|| !!schemaJudgement.blocking` 을 더했다(프로덕션 3파일 + 테스트 2파일). 판정은 **구문만** 본다 — 서버는 `Schema map[string]any`(admin.go:1401)로 받아 `[1,2]`·`"hi"`·`5` 를 400 으로 거절하지만 **`null` 은 통과**하므로(nil map → `json.Marshal` 이 `null`) '객체가 아니면 막는다' 는 규칙은 `null` 에서 화면을 서버보다 좁게 만든다. 「저장」 을 닫는 것이 이 칸에서 정당한 이유는 판정자가 서버가 아니라 **화면 자신의 같은 `JSON.parse`** 여서 요청이 만들어지지도 않기 때문이고, 다른 칸(`name`·`정책`·`Conversion`)이나 다른 화면으로 일반화하지 않았다(모듈 주석에 그 경계를 적었다). 서버·`admin.go`·Go 는 손대지 않았다. 검증: `cd web && npm ci && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build` 전부 통과(테스트 **248 → 259**, +11; 변경 전 248 을 직접 찍어 과제서의 미확인 숫자를 확인했다), `cd sdk && npm ci && npm audit && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build` → `SDK_GATE_EXIT=0`(29/29, `found 0 vulnerabilities`) — ci.yml 에서 web 보다 먼저 도는 게이트라 함께 돌렸다, `go vet ./cmd/... ./internal/...` → `VET_EXIT=0`. 순수 테스트에 더해 **실제 프로덕션 배선**을 확인했다 — `npm run build` 의 dist 를 `/api/v1/me`·`/api/v1/sites`·`/api/v1/event-definitions` 흉내 서버에 올리고 headless Chrome(google-chrome, puppeteer-core 는 /tmp)으로 `/admin?section=schemas` 의 칸을 **실제로 타이핑**해 helperText DOM 과 「저장」 의 `disabled` 를 읽었다(`useUnsavedWarning` 의 `beforeunload` 때문에 사례마다 새 탭). **27건 전부 기대대로**: 깨진 JSON 은 누르지 않아도 오류 색 + 저장 실패 Alert 과 **글자 그대로 같은 문장**이 뜨고 「저장」 이 닫히며 helperText 에 V8 영문 표지(`Unexpected token`·`is not valid JSON`·`position`)가 0개, `{}`·`{"properties":{}}`·`null`·`[1,2]` 네 값은 **막지 않고**(「저장」 열림, 오류 색 없음), 빈 칸은 닫되 칠하지 않고, 이름이 비면 여전히 닫히고(기존 조건을 지우지 않았다), 올바른 값으로 누르면 POST 가 실제로 1건 가고 본문의 `schema` 가 파싱된 객체다. 임시 하네스는 /tmp 에만 두고 `web/dist` 는 커밋 전에 지워 `git status` 로 프로덕션 3 + 테스트 2 파일만 담긴 것을 확인했다. `npx prettier --check` 는 게이트로 쓰지 않았다.
- 실패 재현: 순수 함수 — 먼저 `Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '…/web/src/pages/schemaTextRule.ts'`, 그 다음 **지금 화면과 똑같이 동작하는 항등 스텁**(아무것도 막지 않고 helperText 를 비워 두는 구현)으로 10건 중 **5건 실패** — `not ok 2 - 막는 값은 JSON.parse 가 거절하는 값과 정확히 같다` / `error: "{\"properties\": }" 의 판정이 JSON.parse 와 어긋난다`, `not ok 7 - 빈 칸은 저장을 닫되 오류로 칠하지 않는다` / `error: '"": 저장을 닫지 않았다'`(기존 248건은 스텁에서도 전부 통과 — 새 테스트가 이 칸의 결함만 짚는다는 증거). 프로덕션 배선 — 고친 세 파일을 치우고(`git checkout 992bb75 -- AdminPage.tsx adminErrors.ts`, 새 모듈은 옆으로) main 그대로 재빌드해 같은 브라우저 하네스를 돌리자 **9건 실패**: `FAIL 깨진 JSON: helperText 가 저장 실패 Alert 과 같은 문장 — helper=null`, `FAIL 깨진 JSON: 「저장」 이 닫힌다 — disabled=false`, `FAIL 빈 칸: 「저장」 이 닫힌다 — disabled=false` → `RESULT: 기대와 다름 (9건)`(exit 1). 복원·재빌드 후 같은 하네스가 `RESULT: 전부 기대대로`(27/27). 덧붙여 adminErrors 쪽 단언 1건(실제 `JSON.parse('{"properties": }')` 로 잡은 SyntaxError 의 안내가 `JSON_SCHEMA_RULE` 를 포함한다)은 **변경 전후 모두 통과하는 드리프트 가드**다 — 두 문장이 아직 같으므로 red 가 되지 않는다. 지어내지 않고 그대로 적는다.

「JSON Schema」 칸이 저장 전에 JSON 구문 오류를 말한다

이 칸은 다섯 줄 자유 입력인데 「저장」 이 `!site || !form.name` 만 보았고
helperText 도 없었다. 그래서 깨진 JSON 으로 저장을 누르면 뮤테이션 안의
`JSON.parse(form.schemaText)` 가 던져 요청이 서버에 가지도 않는데, 사용자는
그 헛클릭 왕복을 한 번 치른 뒤에야 안내를 읽었다(브라우저로 재확인 — main
상태에서 클릭 뒤 서버에 도달한 POST 가 0건).

v0.34.57 이 그 뒤늦은 안내를 한국어로 만들었으니 남은 것은 그 문장을 누르기
전에 보여 주는 것뿐이다. cidrRule.ts·retentionRule.ts 선례대로 순수 모듈
schemaTextRule.ts 를 두고, adminErrors.ts 의 JSON 구문 안내와 칸 아래의
helperText 가 같은 상수(JSON_SCHEMA_RULE)를 쓰게 했다 — 글자는 그대로다.

판정은 구문만 본다. 서버는 Schema map[string]any 로 받아 배열·문자열·숫자를
400 으로 거절하지만 null 은 통과시키므로, '객체가 아니면 막는다' 는 규칙은
null 에서 화면을 서버보다 좁게 만든다. 「저장」 을 닫는 것이 이 칸에서
정당한 이유는 판정자가 서버가 아니라 화면 자신의 같은 JSON.parse 여서

The 「망 대역 추가」 form now screens a malformed CIDR before it is sent, which
is the next step after the previous four releases rather than a fifth repeat of
them: those fixed the sentence shown after a failure, and this removes the
failure. The 「CIDR」 box is the only hand-typed CIDR in the console and 「추가」
gated on `!form.name || !form.cidr`, so it only ever stopped an empty box —
10.20.30 with no prefix length, 10.20.30.0/33 out of range, /abc not a number
and 1.2.3.4.5/24 with five octets all crossed the network and came back as the
server's 400 INVALID_CIDR (admin.go:812 net.ParseCIDR), while the box's own
placeholder was showing the right shape directly above it. A new pure module
web/src/pages/cidrRule.ts decides it in the form, following passwordRule.ts in
the same directory. It also moves the sentence that describes correct notation
out of describeNetworkError and into a CIDR_RULE constant both sides read, so
the form's helperText and the INVALID_CIDR Alert say the same thing by
construction; until now that sentence lived only inside adminErrors.ts, which
means a reader could only learn the correct notation *after* getting it wrong.
The server stays the authority and the screen is a mirror of it, so the blocked
set is only what ParseCIDR certainly refuses — a screen stricter than the
server leaves no way to enter a value the server would accept. Host bits to the
right of the netmask pass: 10.20.30.1/24 is not blocked, is not coloured as an
error, and gets a neutral line naming the computed start address instead,
because whether the Postgres `cidr` column refuses what ParseCIDR accepted was
not reproduced against a database here and so is not claimed either way. IPv6
bodies and leading zeros in an IPv4 address pass as well, both being cheaper to
let make one round trip than to risk refusing something valid. Leading zeros in
the prefix length were the place where memory would have been wrong: /024 and
/00000000024 are *accepted* by ParseCIDR, measured by running 29 values through
Go rather than recalled, so the digits are read as a decimal value the way the
server's dtoi reads them and not matched as a shape. Blocking and error colour
are separate states on purpose: an unfinished entry closes the button without
turning the box red, and an untouched form shows the rule rather than a
complaint. Verification went past the pure functions twice. A generated corpus
of 890 values (888 after dedup) was run through both Go ParseCIDR and judgeCIDR:
of the 727 the screen blocks, the server would have accepted none. And the built
dist was served against a stand-in for /api/v1/me, /api/v1/sites and
/api/v1/networks and driven through headless Chrome, reading the button's
disabled state, the helperText DOM, the Mui-error class and the number of POSTs
that reached the server — zero for all four values, and one carrying the typed
value verbatim for 10.20.30.1/24. The same harness against the reverted tree
fails 20 checks and lets 5 POSTs through. The existing word-for-word assertion
on INVALID_CIDR passes unedited. Three production files and one test file, 211
to 223 web tests. 올리지 않고 중립 문구로 되돌린다.

The 「망 대역 추가」 form now screens a malformed CIDR before it is sent, which
is the next step after the previous four releases rather than a fifth repeat of
them: those fixed the sentence shown after a failure, and this removes the
failure. The 「CIDR」 box is the only hand-typed CIDR in the console and 「추가」
gated on `!form.name || !form.cidr`, so it only ever stopped an empty box —
10.20.30 with no prefix length, 10.20.30.0/33 out of range, /abc not a number
and 1.2.3.4.5/24 with five octets all crossed the network and came back as the
server's 400 INVALID_CIDR (admin.go:812 net.ParseCIDR), while the box's own
placeholder was showing the right shape directly above it. A new pure module
web/src/pages/cidrRule.ts decides it in the form, following passwordRule.ts in
the same directory. It also moves the sentence that describes correct notation
out of describeNetworkError and into a CIDR_RULE constant both sides read, so
the form's helperText and the INVALID_CIDR Alert say the same thing by
construction; until now that sentence lived only inside adminErrors.ts, which
means a reader could only learn the correct notation *after* getting it wrong.
The server stays the authority and the screen is a mirror of it, so the blocked
set is only what ParseCIDR certainly refuses — a screen stricter than the
server leaves no way to enter a value the server would accept. Host bits to the
right of the netmask pass: 10.20.30.1/24 is not blocked, is not coloured as an
error, and gets a neutral line naming the computed start address instead,
because whether the Postgres `cidr` column refuses what ParseCIDR accepted was
not reproduced against a database here and so is not claimed either way. IPv6
bodies and leading zeros in an IPv4 address pass as well, both being cheaper to
let make one round trip than to risk refusing something valid. Leading zeros in
the prefix length were the place where memory would have been wrong: /024 and
/00000000024 are *accepted* by ParseCIDR, measured by running 29 values through
Go rather than recalled, so the digits are read as a decimal value the way the
server's dtoi reads them and not matched as a shape. Blocking and error colour
are separate states on purpose: an unfinished entry closes the button without
turning the box red, and an untouched form shows the rule rather than a
complaint. Verification went past the pure functions twice. A generated corpus
of 890 values (888 after dedup) was run through both Go ParseCIDR and judgeCIDR:
of the 727 the screen blocks, the server would have accepted none. And the built
dist was served against a stand-in for /api/v1/me, /api/v1/sites and
/api/v1/networks and driven through headless Chrome, reading the button's
disabled state, the helperText DOM, the Mui-error class and the number of POSTs
that reached the server — zero for all four values, and one carrying the typed
value verbatim for 10.20.30.1/24. The same harness against the reverted tree
fails 20 checks and lets 5 POSTs through. The existing word-for-word assertion
on INVALID_CIDR passes unedited. Three production files and one test file, 211
to 223 web tests. The 「망 대역 추가」 form now screens a malformed CIDR before it is sent, which
is the next step after the previous four releases rather than a fifth repeat of
them: those fixed the sentence shown after a failure, and this removes the
failure. The 「CIDR」 box is the only hand-typed CIDR in the console and 「추가」
gated on `!form.name || !form.cidr`, so it only ever stopped an empty box —
10.20.30 with no prefix length, 10.20.30.0/33 out of range, /abc not a number
and 1.2.3.4.5/24 with five octets all crossed the network and came back as the
server's 400 INVALID_CIDR (admin.go:812 net.ParseCIDR), while the box's own
placeholder was showing the right shape directly above it. A new pure module
web/src/pages/cidrRule.ts decides it in the form, following passwordRule.ts in
the same directory. It also moves the sentence that describes correct notation
out of describeNetworkError and into a CIDR_RULE constant both sides read, so
the form's helperText and the INVALID_CIDR Alert say the same thing by
construction; until now that sentence lived only inside adminErrors.ts, which
means a reader could only learn the correct notation *after* getting it wrong.
The server stays the authority and the screen is a mirror of it, so the blocked
set is only what ParseCIDR certainly refuses — a screen stricter than the
server leaves no way to enter a value the server would accept. Host bits to the
right of the netmask pass: 10.20.30.1/24 is not blocked, is not coloured as an
error, and gets a neutral line naming the computed start address instead,
because whether the Postgres `cidr` column refuses what ParseCIDR accepted was
not reproduced against a database here and so is not claimed either way. IPv6
bodies and leading zeros in an IPv4 address pass as well, both being cheaper to
let make one round trip than to risk refusing something valid. Leading zeros in
the prefix length were the place where memory would have been wrong: /024 and
/00000000024 are *accepted* by ParseCIDR, measured by running 29 values through
Go rather than recalled, so the digits are read as a decimal value the way the
server's dtoi reads them and not matched as a shape. Blocking and error colour
are separate states on purpose: an unfinished entry closes the button without
turning the box red, and an untouched form shows the rule rather than a
complaint. Verification went past the pure functions twice. A generated corpus
of 890 values (888 after dedup) was run through both Go ParseCIDR and judgeCIDR:
of the 727 the screen blocks, the server would have accepted none. And the built
dist was served against a stand-in for /api/v1/me, /api/v1/sites and
/api/v1/networks and driven through headless Chrome, reading the button's
disabled state, the helperText DOM, the Mui-error class and the number of POSTs
that reached the server — zero for all four values, and one carrying the typed
value verbatim for 10.20.30.1/24. The same harness against the reverted tree
fails 20 checks and lets 5 POSTs through. The existing word-for-word assertion
on INVALID_CIDR passes unedited. Three production files and one test file, 211
to 223 web tests.
